source: Meehan (1977) TALE-SPIN, an interactive program that writes stories (IJCAI)
finding: TALE-SPIN simulates characters who solve problems with a planner. Stories come out of simulated rational behaviour. Knowledge areas: plans, physical maps, relationships, personality traits, bodily needs, English output.
numbers: Plans from Schank-Abelson Conceptual Dependency. Four bodily 'sigma-states' (hunger, thirst, rest, sex) start the top-level goals. Relationships: competition, dominance, familiarity, affection, trust, deceit, indebtedness. Traits: kindness, vanity, honesty, intelligence.
quote: Storytelling is a natural language processing activity that requires many kinds of knowledge
limits: Hand-built world model. No evaluation with human raters in this paper.
agent_relevance: A story is a trace of an agent solving a problem. Our scaffold can treat the goal stack plus world model as the source of coherence.

source: Meehan (1977) TALE-SPIN, an interactive program that writes stories (IJCAI)
finding: The 'mis-spun tales' show every missing piece of common knowledge turns into a wrong story: Joe Bear threatens Irving Bird because he does not see that an indirect answer is an answer; Henry Ant drowns because being in water blocks speech and nobody was asked a direct question; 'Gravity' drowned Henry because it had no legs, wings or friends.
numbers: Seven numbered failures are printed. The fix for each was a new rule or fact.
limits: Failures are anecdotal and fixed by hand. This is a classic of knowledge-gap errors.
agent_relevance: Plan-then-simulate systems fail on missing mundane facts. A critic step (S-state check against world facts) targets this kind of error.

source: Meehan (1977) TALE-SPIN, an interactive program that writes stories (IJCAI)
finding: Adding knowledge produced new bugs. Once characters 'noticed' things, the crow noticed the cheese in its mouth, got hungry, and ate it, so the fox had nothing to trick. Another tale looped: Joe asks for a worm to get honey, then for a worm to learn where worms are, and so on. A fox even bargained with himself for the cheese after the cheese fell.
numbers: Looping fix: do not push a goal that is already on the stack. A failed goal is marked, not removed, so it is not retried forever.
quote: don't put a goal on the stack if it's already there
limits: Reported as anecdotes, no counts.
agent_relevance: Direct analogue of loop and repetition guards. Goal-stack duplicates and retry marks are a cheap guardrail pattern.

source: Meehan (1977) TALE-SPIN, an interactive program that writes stories (IJCAI)
finding: Meehan separates a rational narration from a story. 'Joe Bear was famished. He closed his eyes for three seconds. He wasn't hungry any more.' is not rational. 'He ate the honey next to him' is rational but not a story because nothing interesting happened. Stories need a problem with difficulty.
numbers: Difficulty is set partly by the user through character relationships. Aesop morals (e.g. 'Never trust flatterers') are turned into initial world settings so reasonable behaviour yields the moral.
limits: Only simple fables. Moral-to-setup reasoning was done for a handful of morals.
agent_relevance: Interesting output needs a hard enough problem. For creative tasks, the agent can set difficulty on purpose.

source: Binsted and Ritchie (1994) An implemented model of punning riddles
finding: JAPE-1 builds punning riddles from a humour-independent lexicon with two structures. Schemata fix the word relations (fake word made from homonym or substitution). Templates give the surface question-answer form.
numbers: Six schemata in JAPE-1 (e.g. lotus, jumper). Example output: 'What do you get when you cross a sheep and a kangaroo? A woolly jumper.'
limits: Only noun-phrase punchlines. Covers a narrow riddle class.
agent_relevance: Shows a creative system as generic lexical knowledge plus a small set of joke patterns. Separation of 'what to say' from 'how to phrase it'.

source: Binsted and Ritchie (1994) An implemented model of punning riddles
finding: JAPE-1 evaluation: volunteers wrote the lexical entries, so no hand-tuned humour data. 188 jokes were scored by 14 judges on a 0 to 5 scale.
numbers: Mean score 1.5 over 188 jokes. Most scored 1. Nine jokes got a 5 from one judge; the other judge gave those same jokes 0 (3), 1 (3), 2 (3). Some output matched existing jokes (e.g. 'A cereal killer').
limits: Authors say it was not statistically rigorous: few judges, no control group of human-written jokes, jokes seen before.
agent_relevance: Judge disagreement is large for humour. A single rater or single scorer is unreliable.

source: Binsted and Ritchie (1994) An implemented model of punning riddles
finding: Template choice mattered a lot. The 'use syn' template gave non-jokes ('What do you use to hit a waiting line? A pool queue.'). A better template ('What kind of line has sixteen balls?') scored about 2 on average. Vague lexicon classes (hanger = device) scored about 0.5.
numbers: Weak schema-template pairs were to be pruned. Proposed post-production ordering heuristics.
limits: Single early evaluation. Later JAPE and STANDUP work (not opened here) added more tests.
agent_relevance: Generate then filter with a quality ordering. Quality came from the pairing of structure and phrasing, not from the topic.

source: Tearse, Mawhorter, Mateas, Wardrip-Fruin (2011) Experimental results from a rational reconstruction of MINSTREL
finding: First formal test of Turner's 1993 MINSTREL claim that TRAMs (Transform-Recall-Adapt Methods) give creativity. Turner defined creativity as number and quality of differences from similar works. They rebuilt MINSTREL (Minstrel Remixed, Scala) and measured output variance and sensible-to-nonsensical ratio by hand labelling.
numbers: Library of 16 hand-written stories, mean 11.5 nodes, 4 nouns. Seven TRAMs used for the test query. 1000 trials per condition.
quote: Whether or not something is creative depends on the number and quality of its differences from similar works
limits: Rational reconstruction, not original code. Hand labelling by the authors. One main query.
agent_relevance: A test design for creative systems: diversity (variance) against sense. Useful pattern for scoring agent brainstorm output.

source: Tearse, Mawhorter, Mateas, Wardrip-Fruin (2011) Experimental results from a rational reconstruction of MINSTREL
finding: Baseline TRAM system gave variety but poor sense. Only 35.2% of results were sensible.
numbers: Expected differences between two results about 6.90 fields. Sensible/nonsense ratio 0.544. 1000 trials gave 68.8 unique stories, of which 21.0 were sensible. Unique-result ratio 0.439.
limits: Single baseline query. Authors say the default query may be unrepresentative.
agent_relevance: Free recombination gives novelty at the price of nonsense. Needs a sense filter.

source: Tearse, Mawhorter, Mateas, Wardrip-Fruin (2011) Experimental results from a rational reconstruction of MINSTREL
finding: Quality-diversity trade-off is built in. A more constrained query gave far better sense but half the variation. Removing the two most liberal TRAMs (SimilarOutcomes, GeneralizeConstraint) also raised sense and cut variation.
numbers: Alternate query: sense/nonsense 0.947 (unique) and 3.103 (total), expected differences about 3.5 versus 7. Without liberal TRAMs differences about 3 versus 7. Depth limits 3 to 6 were equivalent; depth 2 gave far fewer results; most results sit at depth 2.
limits: Authors say the fix would have to cull nonsense or generate variety without nonsense.
agent_relevance: Matches known novelty-vs-validity trade-off. Our agent should tune breadth and add an explicit validity check, not push one knob.

source: Tearse, Mawhorter, Mateas, Wardrip-Fruin (2011) Experimental results from a rational reconstruction of MINSTREL
finding: Library size matters, and nonsense is easier to make than sense. Removing 8 of 16 stories cut unique results and the sense ratio. The fall in unique results was not proportional to the fall in stories, but the fall in sensible ones was.
numbers: 8 of 16 stories removed at random.
limits: Small library. Random removal only.
agent_relevance: Memory or case-base breadth drives valid novelty. Thin retrieval gives mostly junk recombination.

source: Peinado and Gervas (2006) Minstrel Reloaded: From the magic of Lisp to the formal semantics of OWL
finding: Describes Turner's MINSTREL. It was built in the late 1980s to write short tales (about 200 words) in the King Arthur world. It uses hand-built Lisp frames (the Rhapsody library). Partial re-implementation in OWL showed the frame knowledge can be recast in a standard formalism.
numbers: About 200-word stories. No working original version online at the time.
limits: Partial reimplementation only. No generation results.
agent_relevance: MINSTREL is the model of 'author-level' reasoning: it uses problem-solving about the story itself. Fits our idea of meta goals on top of content goals.

source: Harmon and Jhala (2015) Imaginative recall with story intention graphs
finding: Skald (Tearse) improves MINSTREL's retrieval by weighting TRAM choice instead of random choice. The paper adds Story Intention Graph encodings so Skald output can be told with better language.
numbers: TRAM search failure rate: Minstrel Remixed 19%, Skald 3.5%. TRAMs tried per search: 58 vs 16. TRAMs used when no direct match: 2.4 vs 1.4. MINSTREL has 25 TRAM heuristics.
limits: Speed and retrieval measure only, no human story-quality rating in the table.
agent_relevance: Weighted choice of which transformation to try beats random choice. Same as picking operators by fit.

source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans (2022) Co-writing screenplays and theatre scripts with language models (Dramatron)
finding: Dramatron chains LLM prompts from the top down: log line, then characters, plot, locations, scene-by-scene dialogue. This hierarchy gives long-range coherence. 15 theatre and film professionals each co-wrote a script in a 2-hour session.
numbers: 15 participants, 13 returned the survey. 92% agreed the output was surprising (46% strongly). 77% enjoyed it. 84% found it helpful. 77% felt they collaborated. 61% found it easy. 46% were proud of the result. Over half felt low ownership.
limits: Small N, self-selected industry experts, GPT-3 class model. Film/TV people liked it more than theatre people.
agent_relevance: Hierarchical decomposition with human-editable levels works for long creative output. The plan-then-expand design resembles our S-state flow.

source: Mirowski, Mathewson, Pittman, Evans (2022) Co-writing screenplays and theatre scripts with language models (Dramatron)
finding: Participants said the model loops, repeats, lacks subtext and character motivation, and shows bias. Some liked the glitches as inspiration. Edits showed engagement.
numbers: Repetition score of chosen outputs vs alternatives: Wilcoxon W=57, p=0.467 (no difference, 3 cases). Parallel scene generation caused inconsistency between scenes.
limits: The repetition test is tiny.
agent_relevance: Chained generation needs a consistency pass across independently generated parts.

source: Jentzsch and Kersting (2023) ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny
finding: Asked ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) for a joke 1000 times with 10 prompt wordings. Output was almost all the same few jokes, all existing puns found online.
numbers: 1008 jokes. Over 90% were 25 jokes. 909 were identical to one of the top 25 (917 covered in another passage of the paper). Top four jokes over 50% of output.
limits: Early ChatGPT, Jan-Mar 2023, via web wrapper. Newer models not tested.
agent_relevance: Mode collapse on creative asks. The agent should sample for diversity and check for known-joke recall.

source: Jentzsch and Kersting (2023) ChatGPT is fun, but it is not funny
finding: ChatGPT explained 23 of 25 jokes validly, but gave confident made-up explanations for invalid jokes. In detection tests, removing one joke feature (wordplay, or Q-A structure) made classifications split about evenly. Removing two made all 25 samples 'not a joke'.
numbers: 25 jokes, variant sets of N=19 or 25. Original jokes 100% classified as jokes. Sets A and C mixed. Sets B and D 0 of 25 as jokes.
limits: Manual edits by authors. One model.
agent_relevance: Surface form drives judgment. Do not trust an LLM's explanation as proof it understands.

source: Hessel et al. (2023) Do androids laugh at electric sheep? New Yorker caption contest benchmarks
finding: Three tasks on New Yorker cartoons: match caption to cartoon, rank winning captions, explain the joke. Models trail humans on all three.
numbers: Matching, 5-way: fine-tuned CLIP ViT-L/14 62% vs humans 94% (from pixels). GPT-4 5-shot with human scene descriptions 84.5%. Explanations: human preferred over 5-shot GPT-4 in more than 2/3 of cases.
limits: Language-only models got human-written scene descriptions. Humans were small-N estimates.
agent_relevance: The gap is partly visual and partly cultural knowledge. Better inputs (descriptions) help a lot.

source: Hessel et al. (2023) Do androids laugh at electric sheep? New Yorker caption contest benchmarks
finding: Quality ranking: models beat humans at predicting New Yorker editor picks but lose at predicting crowd picks. Image information helps explanations.
numbers: GPT-3 69.8 vs human estimate 64.6 on editor picks. Crowd picks: GPT-4 73.3 vs human 83.7. T5-11B with image info beats caption-only version in 84.7% of explanation comparisons; T5-11B beats T5-Large in 68.5%.
limits: 3 crowd judges per pair, majority vote. Older models by today's standard.
agent_relevance: Who is the judge changes the result. Define the audience before scoring creativity.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Humor in AI: massive scale crowd-sourced preferences and benchmarks for cartoon captioning
finding: Dataset of over 250 million ratings on over 2.2 million captions from eight years of the contest. GPT-4 and Claude underperform top human entries. Fine-tuning on top-1000 captions (SFT) hurt, RLHF gave less than best-of-N, DPO helped the best-pick win rate.
numbers: Held out 91 of 358 contests, ten captions per contest. Claude-3-Opus captions preferred over the human top-10 by crowd workers 34% of the time (35.4% in table) and by a former New Yorker cartoon editor 1.6%. GPT-4 judge accuracy 67% on rank 1-10 vs 1000-1009 pairs.
limits: Judge is GPT-4 with cartoon descriptions. Preference is for the New Yorker audience.
agent_relevance: Expert and crowd disagree strongly. Best-of-N with a reward model beat RLHF on a subjective task.

source: Horvitz et al. (2024) Getting serious about humor: crafting humor datasets with unfunny LLMs
finding: LLMs are good at removing humour (unfunning) from jokes. GPT-4 edits rate as well as or better than human players and give training data for humor detectors, including code-mixed English-Hindi.
numbers: Context: fewer than 3% of proposed Onion headlines are printed. Original Unfun corpus about 11K headlines. Detailed accuracy tables not extracted here.
limits: I read the abstract, intro and table fragments only; exact accuracies not verified.
agent_relevance: Editing toward a constraint is easier than inventing. Edit-based creation loops are a sound pattern.

source: Gomez-Rodriguez and Williams (2023) A confederacy of models: a comprehensive evaluation of LLMs on creative writing
finding: Same prompt to 12 LLMs and humans: epic single combat of Ignatius J. Reilly and a pterodactyl. 10 creative-writing raters scored 65 stories on a 10-item rubric. Commercial LLMs match or beat the human writers. Humans keep the lead in originality.
numbers: GPT-4 overall 80.2 and top on 8 of 10 items. Best open model (Koala) 60.0. Humor avg 3.4, best 6.5. GPT-4 vs humans on individual metrics p=0.00031. Overall-score t-test: no significant gap for top 6 AI models vs humans. Humans scored 4.9 on epic genre, outscored by 8 LLMs.
limits: Each rater scored a subset. 10 ratings per model. Five human authors. One odd prompt chosen to dodge training data.
agent_relevance: Humour splits models into 'get it' (Claude, Bing, GPT-4) and 'fail'. Structure is the easiest dimension, humor the hardest.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or artifice? LLMs and the false promise of creativity (TTCW)
finding: Introduces TTCW, 14 binary tests drawn from Torrance dimensions (fluency, flexibility, originality, elaboration) for short fiction. 48 stories: 12 by professionals, 36 from ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude 1.3. Over 2,000 expert tests.
numbers: Experts' agreement Fleiss kappa 0.41, aggregate Pearson 0.69. Expert stories passed 84.7% of tests. LLM stories 3 to 10 times less likely to pass. GPT-4 best on originality tests, Claude on fluency, flexibility, elaboration.
limits: Stories about 1400 words, one prompt style, 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Expert human writing beats LLM stories on creativity checklists. Binary checks with rationale are more reliable than Likert.

source: Chakrabarty et al. (2024) Art or artifice? LLMs and the false promise of creativity (TTCW)
finding: LLMs cannot yet act as TTCW judges. Their correlation with expert votes was close to zero.
numbers: Three LLM judges, correlations near zero.
limits: 2023-era judges.
agent_relevance: Do not use an LLM to score creative quality without expert calibration.

source: Marco, Gonzalo, Mateo-Girona (2024) Pron vs Prompt
finding: Award-winning novelist Patricio Pron vs GPT-4 Turbo. 30 titles each, each wrote stories for all 60 titles. Six literary experts scored on a 0-3 rubric. GPT-4 scored lower on all dimensions in English and Spanish.
numbers: Pron creativity mean 1.94, about double GPT-4. Style originality: Pron 1.70, GPT-4 0.36 (Spanish) and 0.63 (English). Experts gave GPT-4 top creativity score on 11 occasions.
limits: One writer, one LLM, temperature 1, different rater groups per language so the language comparison is weak.
agent_relevance: Top humans still lead. The strongest lever was the prompt.

source: Marco, Gonzalo, Mateo-Girona (2024) Pron vs Prompt
finding: Human-chosen titles lift LLM output. GPT-4 scored higher with Pron's titles than its own.
numbers: Gains: style originality +57%, anthology suitability +45%, style attractiveness +30%, own voice +30%. Mann-Whitney p=0.01 (style originality), 0.01 (anthology), 0.04 (theme attractiveness), 0.03 (own voice), 0.06 and 0.15 for others.
limits: Small sample of titles (30).
agent_relevance: Evidence for human-seeded creation. The agent should ask the user for seeds or constraints.

source: Tian et al. (2024) Are LLMs capable of generating human-level narratives?
finding: Discourse-level analysis of stories: arcs, turning points, arousal and valence. LLM stories are uniformly positive, low tension and badly paced. Late turning points (major setback, climax) get too little space.
numbers: 440 narratives of about 706 words. 16 trained annotators. Riches to Rags arc 14.6% in human stories vs 1.3% in GPT-4. Oedipus arc 9.3% vs 1.7%.
limits: Film synopses. Annotation of arcs is subjective.
agent_relevance: LLMs favor happy endings. Prompt for a tension arc.

source: Tian et al. (2024) Are LLMs capable of generating human-level narratives?
finding: Putting discourse features (arc, turning points, affect) into the prompt improves stories.
numbers: Over 40% improvement in diversity, suspense and arousal reported (from abstract).
limits: Automatic and expert measures; exact sub-scores not extracted.
agent_relevance: A plan with turning points inside the prompt is a cheap structural scaffold.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) AARON
finding: AARON is Harold Cohen's program that makes images on its own. Development began 1972 and ended with Cohen's death in 2016. It cannot learn: Cohen hand-coded each new skill. Stages: abstract drawing (1970s), rocks, plants, people (1980s), interior scenes and colour (1990s). Cohen declined to call it creative.
numbers: Moved from C to Lisp in the early 1990s. Whitney Museum showing in 2024. Two drawings shown at the Tate.
limits: Encyclopedia summary. No evaluation data.
agent_relevance: Expertise is coded as explicit knowledge of how marks make an image. Style is fixed. Not evidence for LLM claims.

source: Wikipedia (accessed 2026) David Cope (EMI)
finding: EMI recombines patterns analysed from a composer's work. Cope began it in 1981 after composer's block on an opera commission. Wikipedia says Hofstadter's touring test had audiences guessing Chopin vs EMI-Chopin no better than chance. Cope deleted the EMI database in 2005. Emily Howell later modelled Boden's creativity types.
numbers: EMI about 20,000 lines of Lisp in 2001. Chance-level audience result is stated without N.
limits: Secondary source. The audience result has no sample size here.
agent_relevance: Style imitation by recombination can pass casual listening tests. That shows surface novelty, not a new style.

source: Hofstadter (2001) Staring Emmy straight in the eye and doing my best not to flinch
finding: Known account (not opened this session): Hofstadter reports listeners at music schools could not reliably tell EMI pieces in Bach or Chopin style from human work. Exact N not verified.
numbers: Not recorded because not opened.
limits: Anecdotal staged tests, not controlled experiments. Needs a verified source before use.
agent_relevance: Treat as hearsay in our notes until verified.

source: Turner (1994) The creative process: a computer model of storytelling and creativity
finding: Known (not opened): MINSTREL's author-level goals and TRAMs are the core. Turner defined creativity by the number and quality of differences from similar works. Tearse et al. (2011) and Peinado and Gervas (2006), both opened, quote this.
numbers: See a08-a11 for the tested numbers.
limits: Book not read.
agent_relevance: Use the opened secondary tests, not this line, for claims.

source: Cohen (1979) What is an image? IJCAI
finding: Known (not opened; PDF fetch failed): AARON started from the question of the minimum conditions under which a set of marks functions as an image. The Wikipedia AARON page carries the same framing (a29).
numbers: None.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Same as a29.

source: Ritchie (2001, 2007) Empirical criteria for attributing creativity to a computer program
finding: Ritchie's criteria for creative programs (typicality, quality, novelty ratios) are cited by Tearse et al. (a08) as related measures. Original papers not opened.
numbers: None.
limits: Cited only.
agent_relevance: Good template for scoring: share of outputs that are both typical and high quality.
